intrinsic fluorescence of the individual domains of calmodulation (CaM) can be used to study the effects of site-specific mutations on calcium binding to the domains of CaM and that the calcium-binding properties are altered by mutations of the two arginine residues located between sites II (N-domain) and III (C-domain) of the protein.
we have developed a novel method for studying calcium binding to calmodulation that uses intrinsic fluorescence of phenylalanine in one domain and tyrosine in the other domain of this protein.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural basis for calcium binding to the individual domains of calmodulins.
understanding how CaM binds calcium and targets.
the mechanism of CaM activation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the calcium binding sites in the two domains of CaM are not completely independent of each other, and that the calcium binding site in the N-domain is not completely independent of the calcium binding sites of the C-domain.

the intrinsic fluorescence of the phenylalanine residue in the N-domain and the intrinsic fluorescence of tyrosine residues in the CaM C-domain are useful for monitoring calcium binding to the N-domain and C-domain, respectively.
the fluorescence changes observed in the C-domain of calmodulin are due to calcium binding to sites III and IV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the fluorescence of both tyrosine and phenylalanine in calmodulin can be used to probe the conformational changes associated with calcium binding and that the mutations of the residues in the linker region between sites I and II can alter the calcium binding properties of both domains of calmodulins.

the intrinsic fluorescence of the N-domain of CaM is a sensitive probe of the calcium-binding properties and conformational changes in the N-domain, but the intrinsic fluorescence of both domains can be used to measure the conformational changes associated with calcium binding to the entire protein.
calcium binding to the individual domains of CaM can be monitored with domain-specific intrinsic fluorescence.
